   PLEASE SEND YOUR TEXTFILE!
Text is accepted in any form for
OUTLETTERS: wordprocessor files
(say which),typed or handwritten
letters. However, PLEASE send us
a textfile if possible so your
letter needn't be typed again!
The easiest for us to edit are
Tasword 2 files with the right
margin set at 32 but a textfile
in ANY format is appreciated!

Please state if there should be
parts of your letter you do not
wish published but we always use
our discretion anyway. Letters
may also be edited for clarity
and length... Please ask if you
welcome direct correspondence
from other OUTLET readers and we
will publish your full address.

From: Paul Ledger, YORK




Dear Ron,

Thank you for your letter re-
garding the OUTLET magazine and
the Spectrum Discovery Club. I
had no idea the SDC club had
been disbanded and was expecting
the next newsletter soon. How-
ever, the news did not come as a
great shock as there are only so
many 'disk management' programs
etc, that one can write. I did
not contribute any programs to
the newsletter but being an SDC
member increased my enjoyment of
my spectrum/Opus setup tenfold.


I must confess that I have done
a night class recently for word
processing using Microsoft Wind-
ows and Microsoft Word. This has
opened my eyes as to what's av-
ailable. Whilst I think Tasword
II is an excellent program for
the Spectrum, I am now consider-
ing pensioning them off for a
PC.


Your letter came at an opportune
time as you seem to have a foot
in each camp (Spectrum/PC). I
was looking at the numerous data
files I have compiled using
Tasword II and dreading the task
of having to retype them all on
to a PC machine using MS Word or
MS Works.


As you or some of your subscrib-
ers may have been in the same
situation I wonder if you could
tell me if there is an easy way
of converting Tasword II files
to PC Word or Works compatibil-
ity?  Eventually, when I have
converted all my files, etc. I
will probably dispose of my
Spectrum, Opus, ZX printer and
numerous books, etc. Could you
tell me if there is a market for
these via the OUTLET Spectrum
side of the magazine?

        Yours sincerely,

          Paul Ledger

Brian Cavers to Paul Ledger


Dear Paul,

Many thanks for your letter
regarding OUTLET magazine.

Yes, there are many ways of con-
verting OPUS text files into PC
text files and some are more
difficult than others. A lot
will depend on what OPUS kit you
have - is it a single or double
track diskdrive(40 or 80 track)?
Do you have one or two drives?
Do you have access to, or know
someone with a Disciple/Plus D
set-up? Are all your files on
disks or do you also have them
on cassette audio tapes?


At the PC end, the one thing you
will probably need is the ZX
Spectrum emulator (apart from
anything else, it provides a
nostalgic link from the modern
PC to the Spectrum). The regist-
ered version will also emulate
the Plus D Interface and could
be an important step in trans-
ferring your files as, once at
that stage, we have a utility
that will convert them to PC
ASCII files which can be loaded
into the word processor of your
choice. A tape adapter is also
available which allows files
from Spectrum tapes to be loaded
directly into the emulator and
then converted with our utility.

There is also the possibilty of
a direct link from the Opus to


the PC and we're currently look-
ing at an article by one of our
readers who has done a lot of
transferring files to the PC off
other systems- not partcicularly
the OPUS but he has a wealth of
knowledge in this area and, like
most of us, is always happy to
help a fellow enthusiast.

Regarding the sale of your kit.
A feature of OUTLET is OUTBOARD,
where"For Sale" and "Wanted" ads
are posted (a free facility for
our members) and you can still
see the occasional ad of this
type in MicroMart magazine. Re-
sults are mixed, some things get
snapped up at once and others
have to wait several months -but
there is certainly still a mar-
ket for Spectrum kit.

If you send details of your pre-
sent system and how your files
are stored we can look at the
best option for you while you
decide whether to take the
plunge into the world of the PC.

        Yours sincerely,



          Ron Cavers

want to extract our text. Please
remember it is copyright either
of ourselves or the authors. It
is perfectly alright however, if
you just want a different format
for your own use.          Brian

From:Malcolm Perry,KIDDERMINSTER

Dear Brian.

As a follow on to Colin Bibby
mentioning using the Amstrad
monitor. I use the Amstrad
CTM640 (which is almost identi-
cal to the 644 except it is less
the 12 volt output socket) with
SAM,128K and +2(grey) Spectrums.
The monitor is linear RGB so
reproduces all the SAM colours.
However, I found in general the
SAM output is a bit low to drive
the monitor. This was corrected
by adjusting the internal preset
"SUB BRIGHT" control.The +2A and
+3 have the "SCART" level output
that also combines the Spectrum
"BRIGHT" onto RGB but I have not
personally tried these.

There is however a "minor" prob-
lem with the 128K and +2 (grey)
in that they have TTL RGB levels
as separate BRIGHT output. This
was intended for TTL RGB not
linear/SCART monitors. I found
that the 128/+2 output was a lot
higher than SAM (even before the
internal adjustment) and tended
to overdrive the monitor. This
was reduced so SAM and Spectrums
gave about the same level sig-
nals.


While the RGB will provide basic
colours, the BRIGHT needs to be
superimposed on the RGB signals
to obtain the full Spectrum
range.



It should be remembered there
are a number of differences be-
tween +2 and +2A/+3 RGB connect-
ors which needs consideration if
swapping computers or leads
around. These are:

PIN   +2A/+3           +2
 1     +12V        Comp Video
 3   Audio out       Bright
 5     +12V        Ver. Sync.

The rest are the same for 0V
(earth) and RGB.

On the CTM640 the internal pre-
set level control is situated on
the left hand side about half
way down the PCB looking from
the back. I believe the 644 is
about same position.


Remember however,if removing the
back of the monitor, there are a
lot of high voltage points and
that parts of the switch mode
PSU are live to mains.Use an in-
sulated trimmer to set the pre-
set pot.

I found a reasonable "trial and
error" method was to use SAM on
colour bar test pattern, turn
external brightness fully up,
then adjust internal control so
"black" just starts to brighten
up to grey . This is then reset
to "black" by turning down ext-
ernal control.

The Spectrum colour bar test
pattern could be used in the
same way and will also confirm


that the brightness of each col-
our is about the same and the
difference between BRIGHT and
normal of each colour is distin-
guishable.

One point about the +3 PSU being
set slightly above 5V. In the
48, 128, and +2 Spectrums the
computer is supplied with un-
regulated nominal 9V. The 5V
regulator is in the computer, as
is the dreaded 12V generator
that seems to fail at the drop
of a hat! Therefore there is
negligible conductor length
between 5V reg and processor
circuits hence little volt drop.

The +2A/+3 having the regulators
all built into the PSU and


remote from the computer can
introduce a volt drop in the
connecting lead. I had problems
with the SAM due to this volt
drop and eventually changed the
cable between PSU and computer.

Therefore to ensure the computer
is running at the required 5V it
is not unknown with remote regu-
lated PSUs to set then slightly
high to compensate for losses in
the connecting cable. The volt
drop to some extent negates
having a regulated PSU in the
first place but luckily ICs
accept a small % variation.

When lead volt drop could be a
problem in say industrial situa-
tions, remote sensing, regulated


PSUs are used. A second pair of
wires monitor the voltage at the
load end and automatically adj-
ust the PSU voltage to compens-
ate for the drop. However,that's
another story.

When the +3 PSU is measured at
the connector end without a load
or supplying a lighter load,then
the output may measure higher
than when connected to the comp-
uter.

             Malcolm Perry

From: Malcolm Goodman, LEEDS

Dear Brian/Ron,

If any of your readers who have
a good knowledge of the 48K ROM
would like to cooperate with me
on a machine code program, that
has twice beaten me, then I
would like to hear from them.

Without going into details here,
let me just say that it could
probably be the most practical
routine to be written for the
Speccy - ever. !!??

It could also help to while away
some of those longer winter
nights that are fast approach-
ing.


So come on programmers. If you
are short on ideas then get in
touch. Two heads are better than
one, and three are better than
two.

Now a gripe!!

Has anyone indulged in any PD
software at all?

My experience is that much is
undocumented, leaving you to
guess what a chunk of code actu-
ally does - if you can find the
start address!

And often it has been thrown to-
gether untested, so that error
message result, leaving you to
figure out why.


Then there is a small question
of copyright. I recently tried
some PD material out from a
reputable source. I discovered
to my surprise that one or two
utilities bearing my name and a
copyright symbol were being off-
ered as public domain material.


I've also noted material bear-
ing the OUTLET name doing the
rounds in PD circles.


It is unlikely that I will
pursue the matter through the
courts, but PD librarians,
PLEASE check your programs and
respect copyright!!


It would also help if you actu-
ally tested the programs for
runnability and information as
to what is supposed to happen
before you send stuff out.

              Malcolm Goodman

Brian Cavers to Malcolm Goodman

Hear, Hear to that. However, I
would add that some software
with a copyright symbol is later
declared as PD.There is also the
question of software written by
companies that no longer exist.

The only material in OUTLET that
can be copied is clearly marked
"FREEWARE" or sometimes "PD" or
"PUBLIC DOMAIN". The difference
is that "FREEWARE" means the
author technically retains the
copyright but does not mind the
program being freely copied to
others or for a reasonable fee.

I fully agree that much PD is
obscure and badly documented. We
usually try to clarify it! Brian

From:Bernadette Dowsland,E.YORKS

Dear Ron,

It's that time again, subscript-
ion renewal time, the time when
many readers decide to either
stay or leave Outlet. Now I for
one don't want to leave so on
this occasion I'll give it
another six months' worth but I
feel the mag will have to get
better or this will be the last
renewal.

Let's spell it out.

The golden heyday of Outlet is
long since past as I know you
wouldn't disagree, the question
is how can we improve it in
1997?

On an expensive 3" disc it
seemed good value but not so on
a cheap +D version certainly not
compared with the legendary
Alchnews.

The simple facts are the disc
contains the same files every
month, they just seem to fill up
the disc because there's not
enough else to put on, at least
you now have this letter for
your letters page.

The Disclaimer (a real waste of
space if ever I saw one), New
readers offer file (not a bad
idea, but stick it on every time
and it becomes another space
filler), Outverts(nothing really
wrong except that if the advert-


iser didn't put a date in the
ad, you should have stuck one at
the start. Some of those adverts
are a bit long in the tooth now,
any brand new adverts should at
least be highlighted on the
first month to draw attention to
them being new ones),

The clip art is sometimes good
but quite often it's years old
and done the rounds, the demos
have often been in other PD
libraries yonks and although I
hope the games are well received
by others I also feel I've seen
the same ones too often.


So what are the GOOD bits?...



Well, the readers, letters
surprisingly in fact I enjoyed
the editions that had so many
that you had two files worth.

Also Drivechat, often a good
read. Vaxtrex was one of the
highlights. Sadly,I know I could
not come up with anything so en-
tertaining.

Your Graphics Adventure Creator
conversion was one of your best
achievements of late.

Good utilities are thin on the
ground now.The recent ones also
look familiar with ones in the
PD collections and less useful
than earlier published ones
(exception being DiscDos of
course).

The opening screen has long been
one of the best bits so keep up
the good work there. I've also
enjoyed those big animated
pictures such as the galloping
horses.

You suggested going bi-monthly -
"BUT not yet". NO,I disagree;THE
TIME HAS COME. I need more MEAT
in my copy of OUTLET to justify
the price. Like so many others
although not unemployed, cert-
ainly low paid and with so other
spectrum fanzines around Outlet
has to compete on quality more
than ever.

If nothing else this letter
should lead to some healthy
debate in the letters page over
the next few issues.

The Wetherby Spectrum 'do' took
place on 20th September. It was
not very well advertised or well
attended BUT non the less I was
there and yet again a splendid
effort by all the organisers. BE
AT THE NEXT ONE!

            Bernadette Dowsland

Brian Cavers>Bernadette Dowsland


Thanks for your suggestions and
ideas, Bernadette. We are doing
some heavy thinking here and
await other readers' comments
over the next month or so.

                       Brian

From:Malcolm Perry,KIDDERMINSTER


Dear Brian

As a follow up to my query on
Epson ESC/P and /P2 codes,thanks
to a large brown envelope from
Epson I think the question has
been answered. /P was used for
all their 9 pin printers while
/P2 was for the 24 pin. So as
suspected the /P2 is an extended
version of the original 9 pin
format to allow the extra defi-
nition of 24 pins to be used.

This would mainly be applicable
to graphic modes. Inkjet prin-
ters with the Epson ESC/P2 emu-
lation follow the 24 pin format.


The following is either a pre-
amble or follow up to the info
that all started on Peter John-
sons comments on using INKJET
printers with +D depending which
gets into OUTLET first.

Now it is not for me to recom-
mend any make or model of prin-
ter as I simply do not have per-
sonal experience but it does say
something that on contacting
Hewlett Packard I just got a
list of sources of info most of
which I could not use or could
be costly. However it seemed few
if any HP printers have ESC/P2
emulation.

Cannon have not yet replied at
all and it has been about a
month or more.

Epson replied with a whole wad
of leaflets on their current
range of printers, example col-
our printouts, and I must say
these were excellent. It makes
the colour dump from the LC10
look a bit sick. At first I
thought they were simply bulk
printed photographic copies like
you would get in a colour maga-
zine from perhaps an original
inkjet printout. But, on closer
inspection I am sure they are
actual originals from the print-
ers as the paper is "crinkled"
as it would be on the reverse
side from the wet ink- something
a copy would not be.

There were leaflets describing
how inkjet worked, lists of


accessories like cartridges,
special papers, ribbons and so
on, plus their range of 9 and 24
pin printers and the address of
my local main agent to whom,
incidentally, they passed my
name and they sent through a
price list.

Now obviously Epson are looking
for sales but it does also show
they have some interest in their
products and want to attract
customers. Another consideration
is that I believe Epson help is
free during warranty whereas
Cannon is a premium rate number.

Having waded through a lot of
information from various sources
since the original comment by


Peter Johnson on using inkjet
printers with such as +D my own
personal conclusion is that, yes
inkjets are coming down in price
which makes them a consideration
to purchase. I recently saw some
quite new models secondhand for
`60 - `80.

They obviously in general have
superior quality output to dot
matrix even no doubt if just
running under dot matrix emu-
lation. I consider if using with
+D(or non PC computer) emulation
is the best option.  However, I
have not yet been able to find
out what form the data takes for
such as "designed specifically
for windows" printers use. They
are also quieter.


But there are down sides it
seems to me. They can be far
more expensive to run with the
ink cartridge, although refill-
ing (against maker's advice,
well they would, wouldn't they!)
most likely cut costs somewhat.

Print quality can be affected by
ink and paper type. Special
papers for best results can be
expensive, Some could be "not so
user friendly" if they only have
a 3-colour cartridge, swapping
from 3 colour to black only can
be a pest. Paper handling may
not be so friendly with less
manual control and possibly more
restriction on types of paper,
form paper is in (would I still
be able to use my rolls of cheap
teleprinter paper still?) and

such as strips of labels that
need the indexing perforated
edge to ensure alignment. Hand-
ling ink cartridges on some
makes can be a bit messy with
ink spillage or conversely ink
can clog and so loose print. To
clear this some printers are put
into a "bleed mode" which while
clears the block sends ink into
a waste reservoir and so in eff-
ect wastes ink.

Some do not have a "draft" mode
so use as much ink for every
print which can get through a
lot of ink if doing a number of
test prints to get something
right. A worn out ink ribbon can
still often be used for rough
tests, an empty ink cartridge
cannot!

It is unlikely all the points
above will happen to any one
printer but I still consider
that unless the need for the
higher quality is essential.
That unless you are using a PC
where you can load the correct
driver then a lot of the high
quality graphics facilities are
lost. If you are mainly using
the printer for programme list-
ing, MC debugging,the odd letter
and so on, the dot matrix still
seems the more cost effective,
user-friendly option. Now all
this is based on what I have
read, I leave it to those who
actually have, have access to or
use inkjet printers to give the
practical side of using and per-
haps even prove me wrong.
                  Malcolm Perry

From: Thomas Eberle, GERMANY


Hello Spec-Chums!

After a long summer period where
we all were on holidays or other
wise - but not in front of our
beloved Spectrum - let's have
another look what's going on...

Spectrum meetings - name them
'Fairs' or 'Coms' - are very
pleasant these days. Well, there
was in Petersburg (Russia) the
famous 'Englight-Party 97' and
another 'com' was near Prague
(Czech Republic). But one of the
best meetings I was ever at, was
in Germany: the SPC-Meeting in
Munchengladbach...


At the SPC-Meeting,not only were
there about 50 people in two
days looking and talking, there
were also a lot of things to buy
or to see.  Visitors could see,
for example, the famous Russian
PENTAGON: a Spectrum clone, only
much faster, or the well-known
but not often seen disc inter-
face MB02+ which shows its new
features very well presented.
There were also others from the
ZX scene, normally working on
the ZX81, they also had some
ideas for the Speccy. So, to me
was shown an LCD interface to
connect LCD screens (for example
from a laptop) to the Speccy. It
is really working:without colour
and a little bit slow - but the
inventor promised to make a new,
faster version.

A lot of bargains were also
there to be had: monitors, disc
interfaces,Multifaces and Micro-
drives for really cheap prices.
For every Spectrum- dedicated
user, this was heaven.


Some other shows planned are...



15th Nov: Filderstadt, Germany
          The International
          Sinclair Meeting.



Nov/Dec   Zlin (Czech Republic)
          Zlincom 97.



Two clubs are joining forces. In
1998 the Spectrum-User-Club and
the Austrian-Spectrum-Club will
release the SUC-Session magazine
together. Nowadays the ASC does
the disc magazine SCENE+ and the
SUC does the paper magazine
SUC-SESSION, both monthly. Next
year, SUC-SESSION will come out
bi-monthly but with more power
and with SCENE+ as a cover disc
(for +D/Disciple,Opus Discovery,
MB02+ or tape) Price is 50,00 DM
per year or 10,00 DM a single
issue. If interested write to...

   Spectrum-User-Club,
   Rainackerstr. 4,
   70794 Filderstadt, Germany.
   Tel/Fax: ++49/(0)711-775033
   Email: Sintech@online.de


As you can see in the preceding,
Sintech is also now on the 'net.
Look at their newest offers at:

http://www.online.de/home/
                         sintech

Thanks a lot and till next time,

                  Thomas Eberle

Many thanks, Thomas. It's good
to hear the Spectrum scene is

Dear Brian.

As a follow on to Colin Bibby mentioning using the Amstrad monitor. I use the Amstrad CTM640 (which is almost identi- cal to the 644 except it is less the 12 volt output socket) with SAM,128K and +2(grey) Spectrums. The monitor is linear RGB so reproduces all the SAM colours. However, I found in general the SAM output is a bit low to drive the monitor. This was corrected by adjusting the internal preset "SUB BRIGHT" control.The +2A and +3 have the "SCART" level output that also combines the Spectrum "BRIGHT" onto RGB but I have not personally tried these.

There is however a "minor" prob- lem with the 128K and +2 (grey) in that they have TTL RGB levels as separate BRIGHT output. This was intended for TTL RGB not linear/SCART monitors. I found that the 128/+2 output was a lot higher than SAM (even before the internal adjustment) and tended to overdrive the monitor. This was reduced so SAM and Spectrums gave about the same level sig- nals.

While the RGB will provide basic colours, the BRIGHT needs to be superimposed on the RGB signals to obtain the full Spectrum range.

It should be remembered there are a number of differences be- tween +2 and +2A/+3 RGB connect- ors which needs consideration if swapping computers or leads around. These are:

```text
PIN   +2A/+3           +2
```

1     +12V        Comp Video 3   Audio out       Bright 5     +12V        Ver. Sync.

The rest are the same for 0V (earth) and RGB.

On the CTM640 the internal pre- set level control is situated on the left hand side about half way down the PCB looking from the back. I believe the 644 is about same position.

Remember however,if removing the back of the monitor, there are a lot of high voltage points and that parts of the switch mode PSU are live to mains.Use an in- sulated trimmer to set the pre- set pot.

I found a reasonable "trial and error" method was to use SAM on colour bar test pattern, turn external brightness fully up, then adjust internal control so "black" just starts to brighten up to grey . This is then reset to "black" by turning down ext- ernal control.

The Spectrum colour bar test pattern could be used in the same way and will also confirm

that the brightness of each col- our is about the same and the difference between BRIGHT and normal of each colour is distin- guishable.

One point about the +3 PSU being set slightly above 5V. In the 48, 128, and +2 Spectrums the computer is supplied with un- regulated nominal 9V. The 5V regulator is in the computer, as is the dreaded 12V generator that seems to fail at the drop of a hat! Therefore there is negligible conductor length between 5V reg and processor circuits hence little volt drop.

The +2A/+3 having the regulators all built into the PSU and

remote from the computer can introduce a volt drop in the connecting lead. I had problems with the SAM due to this volt drop and eventually changed the cable between PSU and computer.

Therefore to ensure the computer is running at the required 5V it is not unknown with remote regu- lated PSUs to set then slightly high to compensate for losses in the connecting cable. The volt drop to some extent negates having a regulated PSU in the first place but luckily ICs accept a small % variation.

When lead volt drop could be a problem in say industrial situa- tions, remote sensing, regulated

PSUs are used. A second pair of wires monitor the voltage at the load end and automatically adj- ust the PSU voltage to compens- ate for the drop. However,that's another story.

When the +3 PSU is measured at the connector end without a load or supplying a lighter load,then the output may measure higher than when connected to the comp- uter.

Malcolm Perry

Dear Brian

As a follow up to my query on Epson ESC/P and /P2 codes,thanks to a large brown envelope from Epson I think the question has been answered. /P was used for all their 9 pin printers while /P2 was for the 24 pin. So as suspected the /P2 is an extended version of the original 9 pin format to allow the extra defi- nition of 24 pins to be used.

This would mainly be applicable to graphic modes. Inkjet prin- ters with the Epson ESC/P2 emu- lation follow the 24 pin format.

The following is either a pre- amble or follow up to the info that all started on Peter John- sons comments on using INKJET printers with +D depending which gets into OUTLET first.

Now it is not for me to recom- mend any make or model of prin- ter as I simply do not have per- sonal experience but it does say something that on contacting Hewlett Packard I just got a list of sources of info most of which I could not use or could be costly. However it seemed few if any HP printers have ESC/P2 emulation.

Cannon have not yet replied at all and it has been about a month or more.

Epson replied with a whole wad of leaflets on their current range of printers, example col- our printouts, and I must say these were excellent. It makes the colour dump from the LC10 look a bit sick. At first I thought they were simply bulk printed photographic copies like you would get in a colour maga- zine from perhaps an original inkjet printout. But, on closer inspection I am sure they are actual originals from the print- ers as the paper is "crinkled" as it would be on the reverse side from the wet ink- something a copy would not be.

There were leaflets describing how inkjet worked, lists of

accessories like cartridges, special papers, ribbons and so on, plus their range of 9 and 24 pin printers and the address of my local main agent to whom, incidentally, they passed my name and they sent through a price list.

Now obviously Epson are looking for sales but it does also show they have some interest in their products and want to attract customers. Another consideration is that I believe Epson help is free during warranty whereas Cannon is a premium rate number.

Having waded through a lot of information from various sources since the original comment by

Peter Johnson on using inkjet printers with such as +D my own personal conclusion is that, yes inkjets are coming down in price which makes them a consideration to purchase. I recently saw some quite new models secondhand for

```text
`60 - `80.
```

They obviously in general have superior quality output to dot matrix even no doubt if just running under dot matrix emu- lation. I consider if using with +D(or non PC computer) emulation is the best option.  However, I have not yet been able to find out what form the data takes for such as "designed specifically for windows" printers use. They are also quieter.

But there are down sides it seems to me. They can be far more expensive to run with the ink cartridge, although refill- ing (against maker's advice, well they would, wouldn't they!) most likely cut costs somewhat.

Print quality can be affected by ink and paper type. Special papers for best results can be expensive, Some could be "not so user friendly" if they only have a 3-colour cartridge, swapping from 3 colour to black only can be a pest. Paper handling may not be so friendly with less manual control and possibly more restriction on types of paper, form paper is in (would I still be able to use my rolls of cheap teleprinter paper still?) and

such as strips of labels that need the indexing perforated edge to ensure alignment. Hand- ling ink cartridges on some makes can be a bit messy with ink spillage or conversely ink can clog and so loose print. To clear this some printers are put into a "bleed mode" which while clears the block sends ink into a waste reservoir and so in eff- ect wastes ink.

Some do not have a "draft" mode so use as much ink for every print which can get through a lot of ink if doing a number of test prints to get something right. A worn out ink ribbon can still often be used for rough tests, an empty ink cartridge cannot!

It is unlikely all the points above will happen to any one printer but I still consider that unless the need for the higher quality is essential. That unless you are using a PC where you can load the correct driver then a lot of the high quality graphics facilities are lost. If you are mainly using the printer for programme list- ing, MC debugging,the odd letter and so on, the dot matrix still seems the more cost effective, user-friendly option. Now all this is based on what I have read, I leave it to those who actually have, have access to or use inkjet printers to give the practical side of using and per- haps even prove me wrong. Malcolm Perry

В продолжение темы использования монитора Amstrad, поднятой Colin Bibby: я использую Amstrad CTM640 (который практически идентичен 644-му, за исключением отсутствия разъёма питания 12 В) с компьютерами SAM, 128K и +2 (серый) Spectrum. Монитор имеет линейный вход RGB, поэтому воспроизводит всю палитру SAM. Однако я обнаружил, что в целом выходной сигнал SAM слабоват для раскачки монитора. Это удалось исправить подстройкой внутреннего подстроечника «SUB BRIGHT». У +2A и +3 уровень сигнала соответствует стандарту SCART и сигнал «BRIGHT» подмешивается прямо в RGB, но лично я их не пробовал.

Однако со 128K и +2 (серым) есть «небольшая» проблема: у них уровни TTL RGB и отдельный выход BRIGHT. Это предназначалось для мониторов TTL RGB, а не линейных/SCART. Я выяснил, что сигнал со 128/+2 был намного сильнее, чем с SAM (даже до внутренней регулировки), и монитор перегружался. Уровень был снижен, так что SAM и Spectrum стали давать примерно одинаковый сигнал.

Хотя RGB обеспечивает основные цвета, сигнал BRIGHT должен накладываться на линии RGB для получения полной палитры Спектрума.

Следует помнить, что между разъёмами RGB у моделей +2 и +2A/+3 есть ряд различий, которые необходимо учитывать при замене компьютеров или кабелей:

```text
PIN   +2A/+3           +2
 1     +12V        Comp Video
 3   Audio out       Bright
 5     +12V        Ver. Sync.
```

Остальные контакты (0V/земля и RGB) совпадают.

На CTM640 внутренний подстроечный резистор расположен с левой стороны примерно посередине платы, если смотреть сзади. Полагаю, на 644-м он находится примерно там же.

Помните, однако, что при снятии задней крышки монитора открывается множество точек с высоким напряжением, а части импульсного блока питания находятся под напряжением электросети! Для регулировки подстроечного резистора используйте изолированную отвёртку.

Вполне разумным методом «проб и ошибок» оказалось подать с SAM тестовую таблицу цветовых полос, выкрутить внешнюю яркость на максимум, а затем отрегулировать внутренний резистор так, чтобы «чёрный» цвет только-только начал светлеть до серого. Затем внешним регулятором яркость снова убирается до нормального «чёрного».

Тестовую таблицу цветов Спектрума можно использовать точно так же — она позволит убедиться, что яркость каждого цвета примерно одинакова, а разница между BRIGHT и нормальным цветом хорошо различима.

Ещё один момент по поводу блока питания +3, выдающего чуть больше 5 В. В моделях 48, 128 и +2 в компьютер подаётся нестабилизированное напряжение номиналом 9 В. Стабилизатор на 5 В стоит внутри компьютера, как и тот ужасный генератор на 12 В, который, кажется, выходит из строя от малейшего чиха! Поэтому проводники между стабилизатором 5 В и схемами процессора имеют ничтожную длину, и падение напряжения минимально.

У моделей +2A/+3 все стабилизаторы вынесены в блок питания и находятся вдали от компьютера, что может вызывать падение напряжения в соединительном проводе. У меня были проблемы с SAM из-за этой просадки, и в итоге пришлось заменить кабель между БП и компьютером.

Поэтому, чтобы компьютер гарантированно получал положенные 5 В, при внешних стабилизаторах нередко выставляют чуть завышенное напряжение для компенсации потерь в соединительном кабеле. Падение напряжения до некоторой степени сводит на нет саму суть использования стабилизированного БП, но, к счастью, микросхемы терпят небольшие отклонения в процентах.

Когда падение напряжения в проводах становится критичным (например, в промышленности), используются стабилизированные блоки питания с выносными датчиками (remote sensing). Вторая пара проводов отслеживает напряжение непосредственно на нагрузке и автоматически корректирует выход БП для компенсации потерь. Но это уже совсем другая история.

Если же измерять напряжение на разъёме БП от +3 без нагрузки или с облегчённой нагрузкой, то на выходе значение может оказаться выше, чем при подключении к компьютеру.

Недавно я видел несколько довольно новых подержанных моделей за `60 - `80.

Они, очевидно, в целом выдают более качественный результат по сравнению с матричными, даже без сомнения просто работая в режиме матричной эмуляции. Я считаю, что при использовании с +D (или компьютерами не PC) эмуляция — лучший вариант. Однако мне пока не удалось выяснить, какой формат данных используется принтерами, «разработанными специально для Windows». Кроме того, они работают тише.

Но, как мне кажется, есть и обратная сторона. Они могут обходиться гораздо дороже в эксплуатации из-за чернильного картриджа, хотя перезаправка (вопреки советам производителя — ну а что еще они скажут!), скорее всего, несколько снизит затраты.

На качество печати могут влиять тип чернил и бумаги. Специальная бумага для достижения наилучших результатов может быть дорогой. Некоторые модели могут оказаться «не очень удобными для пользователя», если у них установлен только 3-цветный картридж: замена 3-цветного на чисто черный может стать морокой. Работа с бумагой может оказаться менее удобной из-за меньшего ручного контроля и, возможно, больших ограничений по типам бумаги, форме, в которой она подается (смогу ли я по-прежнему использовать свои рулоны дешевой телетайпной бумаги?), а также лентам с наклейками, которым требуется перфорированный край для позиционирования. Обращение с чернильными картриджами на некоторых марках может быть слегка грязным из-за проливания чернил, или наоборот — чернила могут засыхать и приводить к пропускам при печати. Чтобы это устранить, некоторые принтеры переводятся в режим прочистки («bleed mode»), который, хоть и прочищает засор, сливает чернила в резервуар для отходов и, таким образом, фактически тратит чернила впустую.

У некоторых нет чернового режима («draft»), поэтому они тратят одинаковое количество чернил на каждый отпечаток, из-за чего может уйти много чернил при выполнении серии пробных распечаток для подгонки результата. Изношенную красящую ленту все еще часто можно использовать для черновых тестов, пустой чернильный картридж — нельзя!

Маловероятно, что все упомянутые проблемы возникнут у какого-то одного принтера, но я по-прежнему считаю, что если только вам жизненно не необходимо повышенное качество печати... И если вы не работаете на PC, где можно загрузить правильный драйвер, то многие из преимуществ качественной графики просто теряются. Если вы в основном используете принтер для распечатки листингов программ, отладки машинного кода, редких писем и тому подобного, матричный принтер все еще кажется более экономичным и удобным для пользователя вариантом. Все это, конечно, основано на том, что я читал, поэтому я оставляю слово за теми, у кого струйные принтеры действительно есть, у кого есть к ним доступ или кто пользуется ими, чтобы они осветили практическую сторону вопроса и, возможно, доказали, что я неправ.
